MINE FINDERS, INC.
8700 WEST 14TH AVENUE LAKEWOOD, COLORADO 80215 (303) 233-0585
July 12, 1972
44
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Room 4410
Department of Interior
Washington, D.C. 20240
Dear Sir:
I am writing to express my concern for legislation or regulation which may come about as a result of executive order 11644 regarding the use of off-road vehicles — Draft Environmental Statement, Int DES 72 - 62, May 26, 1972, notice of which I understand appeared in the Federal Register June 2.
I am a professional geologist with two graduate degrees and have worked in the field for about 24 years. I was employed by the U.S. Geological Survey on both full-time and part-time bases from 1948 to 1955 and worked in Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona. For the last 17 years I have been a mining and exploration geologist and was fortunate enough, while in the employee of the Climax Molybdenum Company, to participate in two major mineral discoveries. For the last two and one-half years I have been working for a small company, of which I am the president, engaged in contract exploration in western North America for a major raw material company. We now have a staff of seven full-time geologists plus supporting personnel, and hope to add one or two more people during the next eighteen months.
As a geologist and one who enjoys and appreciates nature, I share your concern for the degradation of our remaining "wild lands" by the indiscriminate use or over use by off-road vehicles. On the other hand I am very much alarmed about some of the proposed restrictions on the use of such vehicles viewed from the position of one who finds them essential for the efficient conduct of his business. I am not familiar with all of the proposed regulations but understand that a four month advance notice would be required for the application of a permit for an off-road vehicle event. It is literally impossible for us to predict four months in advance a specific or, in many cases, even a general off-road vehicle usage. Thus, I am fearful that such restrictions rigidly enforced would greatly reduce our chances of success in making a mineral discovery and in properly locating it according to existing laws governing the location of mineral claims. I might add that mineral exploration is a particularly hazardous business at best and that the odds are great against making a significant find.
